newsitem.title: ITALY: Versace seen as hot item if he cashes in on cachet.
newsitem.headline: Versace seen as hot item if he cashes in on cachet.

text.p: Italy's Gianni Versace, long-time designer to the stars, is likely to become the latest fashion in finance if he goes ahead with plans to offer his clothing empire to the stock market, analysts said on Wednesday.

While the Versace company confirms only that he is considering listing sometime in the future, the possibility has been mooted strongly by his brother and business manager Santo Versace in recent newspaper interviews.

Timing and details remain vague for now, but analysts say after the successful 1995 flotations of Italian luxury goods group Gucci and jewellers Bulgari, a newcomer like Versace would be an upbeat addition to an expanding sector of cachet names.
"They are very much in vogue," said a London analyst who declined to be named. "But it is a question of a company like this being taken up for its own merit, if it can show growth."

"These companies have good growth and profitability and someone like Versace is fairly transparent, unlike other companies which have originated from designers," said another investment analyst who asked not to be named.

Santo Versace, chairman of the Gianni Versace group, told the Italian daily Il Sole earlier in March a planned flotation for the end of 1997 had been put off until June 1998 to allow the company to finish restructuring.
He said the group was interested in a listing in Milan and on Wall Street, had cut prices for the last three seasons and would continue to do so as it prepared for listing.
Versace, whose clients include Britain's Princess Diana and actress Elizabeth Hurley, saw sales up 23.5 percent in 1996 to 845 billion lire ($500 million), with 80 percent sold abroad.
Analysts said Gucci and Bulgari had reassured wary investors with their performances after listing, while designer clothing and luxury goods were enjoying a growth period.
This was driven by wealth sprouting up in Asian and former communist economies, lower birth-rates but higher disposable incomes in others, and globe-trotting shoppers buying duty free.
Consumers, unable to gauge standards from competitive pricing at the lower end of the market, are turning to costlier, famous-name items synonymous in their minds with quality.
And the 1980s snob factor is back as consumers flash their wealth. "More women with their own disposable income are proud to buy themselves a Prada handbag," the investment analyst said.
Getting the balance right to tap this last trend is crucial.
Paul Gordon, luxury goods analyst at investment house IMI-Sigeco, said firms had to be careful making products affordable but exclusive.
But risk exists. "Fashion is fashion. Consumer trends are trends and they could be subject to economic change," the investment analyst said.
"If the name goes out of fashion it hits hard," Gordon said.
The secret is a mix of designer wear and designer goods.

Gordon said Gucci, as a mainly luxury goods producer, has 15 percent of turnover in clothing. A rave fashion review might bring in shoppers but even if that season's styles don't provoke a sale, a kudos-carrying Gucci bag remains a staple purchase.
In Versace's case, Il Sole reports just over 50 percent of turnover is in clothing, while accessories account for 25 percent, perfumes 15 and household furnishings four percent.

So while Versace was originally pure fashion, the group has solidly increased its own-label accessories, the investment analyst said, adding: "Most of these designers are not now just focusing on a single product."
